headline: Correct answers can hide broken reasoning
intro: I adapted a tiered reasoning pipeline to XLNet to ask a harder question than story classification: can a model identify the conflicting sentences and physical states that justify its choice?
context: University of Michigan · Natural-language-processing course project · Sept–Dec 2021
role: XLNet-base integration, fine-tuning, loss-function ablations, evaluation, and final report.

hero.alt: An illustrative glass-breaking story is mapped to three evaluation levels: story choice, conflicting sentences, and physical states.
hero.caption: The three levels of TRIP reasoning. The short glass story is an illustrative explanation, not a dataset example or saved model prediction.

metrics.label: Supervision signals
metrics.note: Preconditions, effects, conflicts, and story choice.

metrics.label: Story accuracy
metrics.note: Validation result with state-classification losses omitted.

question.title: What does a correct story choice actually prove?
question.text: TRIP pairs plausible and implausible stories about physical situations. A useful evaluation should reveal whether the model understands the conflict, alongside whether it chooses the right story.

steps.title: Adapt the model
steps.text: Integrated Hugging Face XLNet-base-cased into the published TRIP pipeline, including its tokenizer, model configuration, and representations.

steps.title: Change supervision
steps.text: Fine-tuned the model and evaluated loss ablations across story choice, conflicting-sentence detection, and physical-state preconditions and effects.

steps.title: Evaluate the explanation
steps.text: Compared validation accuracy with consistency and verifiability, which require progressively stronger evidence behind the story choice.

finding.title: 80% accuracy. 0% verifiable reasoning.
finding.text: Omitting state-classification losses increased reported story accuracy from 76.7% to 80.0%, while consistency fell from 12.7% to zero. Neither configuration produced verifiable reasoning in this validation table. Final-answer accuracy alone missed that failure.

charts.title: The answer–explanation gap
charts.subtitle: XLNet validation results from Table 1 of the December 2021 course report. Higher is better; the measures have different requirements.

details: Accuracy counts correct story choices. Consistency also requires identifying the conflicting sentence pair; verifiability additionally requires the relevant physical-state predictions.
These are historical report results, not a new benchmark run. The archived notebook corroborates the XLNet adaptation; no statistical-significance claim is made from the two reported configurations.
credits: The TRIP dataset, tiered reasoning framework, and original pipeline are by Storks and colleagues. My modified notebook is preserved in the linked public fork.
BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa comparisons in my report are baselines reported by Storks et al., not independent reruns. The hero diagram is a new conceptual illustration of the evaluation task.
